title: One-Way Quantum Symmetric Private Information Retrieval Protocol From A Single Database Server Using NISQ Devices
abstract: Symmetric private information retrieval (SPIR) lets an inquirer obtain one specific bit only, without leaking any information about its index to the database owner. With a single server, this is impossible for parties with unrestricted quantum power. We show that it becomes possible, with information-theoretic security, when the server and the user hold only noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices without long-term quantum memory and measure each qubit on arrival, while the eavesdropper remains all-powerful; this is a stricter form of the memory restriction of the bounded- and noisy-quantum-storage models. The server sends BB84 states one way; the user discriminates them unambiguously and so knows a random subset of the bits. After a joint random permutation into blocks, the user announces the conclusive locations of one privately chosen block, and the server hashes and takes a random parity of these locations in every block; the permutation makes it exponentially unlikely that one set of locations fits two blocks. We prove secrecy against the eavesdropper, database privacy through an explicit size rule for the announced set, and user privacy against a server who prepares the prescribed BB84 states and announces truthfully, exactly for single photons and up to a small multi-photon term over a tolerated noise channel. The only addition to BB84 equipment is a passive linear-optical measurement with one ancillary mode. For a $10^{4}$-bit database and database privacy $10^{-6}$, blocks of about a thousand qubits suffice over a tolerated noise channel for a user who applies the prescribed measurement; certifying an arbitrary memoryless user and committing to the permutation need larger auxiliary transmissions, which we quantify with finite keys. Database privacy extends to decoy-state weak coherent pulses, and simulations show that the bound is nearly tight.
summary: This paper presents a quantum protocol for Symmetric Private Information Retrieval (SPIR) that works even when the communicating parties are limited to noisy, memory-less NISQ devices. It achieves information-theoretic security by leveraging BB84 states and random permutations. This work is significant because it provides a practical, resource-constrained solution to a fundamental problem in quantum data access.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of achieving Symmetric Private Information Retrieval (SPIR) from a single database server using quantum communication.
main_result: It demonstrates that provably secure QSPIR is possible under the strict constraint of NISQ devices, requiring only passive linear-optical measurements alongside standard QKD components.
method: The protocol combines principles from Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) with cryptographic techniques like random permutations and hashing to ensure index privacy.
model_or_system: The system utilizes single photons transmitting BB84 states over a one-way quantum channel. The security analysis is tailored for the NISQ regime, meaning no long-term quantum memory is assumed for the communicating parties.
key_observables: Secrecy against eavesdroppers, database privacy (quantified by an explicit size rule), and user privacy.
important_parameters: Database size ($10^4$-bit example), required database privacy ($10^{-6}$), and block size (around a thousand qubits).
main_assumptions: The security proof assumes the eavesdropper is all-powerful, while the user and server are restricted to NISQ devices. The protocol is shown to work for single photons over a tolerated noise channel.
figures_summary: Figure 6 validates the effective Unambiguous State Discrimination (USD) rates against signal intensity ($\mu_1$) and transmittance ($\eta$), while Figure 7 compares measured conclusive counts for the honest receiver versus an adversary using Monte Carlo simulations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem, details a multi-step protocol involving BB84 transmission, joint random permutation, and hashing. It then provides security proofs and validates the resource requirements using simulation and theoretical bounds.
why_interesting: The focus on NISQ constraints and the integration of quantum communication security with information retrieval makes it highly relevant for quantum optics and quantum information theorists designing practical quantum protocols.
